pages.title: The DC compound motor
pages.for: Heavy loads that come and go, such as presses and shears. A series field adds torque under load. A shunt field holds a definite no-load speed.
pages.rule:
Shunt field across the supply. Series field in line with the armature.
Cumulative: flux = shunt part + series part × Ia.
Torque goes with flux × Ia. Speed goes with back-emf E ÷ flux.

Starting torque at the same current: series most, compound next, shunt least.
Running light: series runs away. Compound rises to a definite speed. Shunt barely moves.
Speed regulation: shunt best, compound between, series worst. Use the maker's figure.
Used for: series for hoists and traction. Shunt for steady speed. Compound for presses and shears.
Reverse it: swap the armature leads, or both fields.

traps.text: Differential can be unstable. If the speed rises as load goes on, suspect the series field opposing the shunt field.
traps.cite: [^13] [^14] [^15] [^16] DC compound motor sheet; MTU chapter 11; electrotechnik; electricaleasy

traps.text: After a rewind, check the series field polarity against the maker's diagram. Never find it by running the motor light at full voltage.
Reverse it by swapping the armature leads, or both fields. Swapping one field alone makes it differential.
Do not use it for wide speed control by weakening the shunt field. The no-load speed can get very high.
Isolate, lock off and prove dead. Then megger to frame, measure each winding's resistance, and check the brushes and commutator.

pages.where: Punch presses, shears, crushers and reciprocating compressors, often with a flywheel.

pages.name: How it works
pages.text:
A compound motor has two field windings. It starts harder than a shunt motor, yet settles at a definite speed running light.

The shunt field sits across the supply. The series field is in line with the armature.

If the fields aid, it is cumulative compound. Only the series part of the flux grows with the load.

Reverse the series field and the fields oppose. That is differential compound, rarely used as it can be unstable.

This is long shunt. Short shunt puts the shunt field across the armature only.
pages.alt: DC supply line current armature current field current shunt field series field fields aid: cumulative fields oppose: differential armature

pages.name: Between shunt and series
pages.text: At 0% it is a shunt motor: 1.050 running light, and a torque of 2.00 at twice rated current. At 15% the shunt field is smaller, so there is less flux running light. The series part adds flux under load. The no-load speed rises to 1.224 and the torque to 2.30. At 100% it is a series motor, and running light it runs away. On Differential at 15%, the speed rises with load, from 0.919 to 1.115. The torque falls to 1.70.
pages.alt: Then switch to Differential. Torque goes with flux × Ia. Speed goes with back-emf ÷ flux. DC supply line current Ia field current shunt field series field fields aid: cumulative fields oppose: differential armature Flux running light 0.8575 Flux at 2.00 × rated current 1.15 0 1.00 rated 2.00 On Differential the share stops at 50%.
pages.html:
Then switch to Differential.

Torque goes with flux × Ia. Speed goes with back-emf ÷ flux.

On Differential the share stops at 50%.

No-load speed, per unit1.224
Speed regulation22.4%
Torque, 2.00 × rated current2.30

With a 15% series share, the flux running light falls to 0.8575. So it runs light faster, at 1.224. At twice rated current the flux rises to 1.15, so the torque there rises to 2.30.

Worked in per unit, where 1.00 is rated volts, current, flux, speed and torque

Assume the armature circuit drops 5% of the supply at rated current. Running light, it draws 0.05 of rated current. Both are examples.

Flux = shunt part + series part × Ia, or minus it on Differential.

Back-emf = 1 − 0.05 × Ia. That is the supply less the drop. Speed = back-emf ÷ (0.95 × flux). 0.95 is the back-emf at rated current. Dividing by it makes rated speed 1.00.

Running light, Ia = 0.05: back-emf = 1 − 0.05 × 0.05 = 0.9975. Then 0.9975 ÷ 0.95 = 1.05, for every share.

Compound, 15%: flux running light = 0.85 + 0.15 × 0.05 = 0.8575. No-load speed = 1.05 ÷ 0.8575 = 1.224. Regulation (1.224 − 1.000) ÷ 1.000 = 22.4%. Flux at 2.00 = 0.85 + 0.15 × 2.00 = 1.15. Torque = 1.15 × 2.00 = 2.30. Speed at 2.00 = 0.90 ÷ (0.95 × 1.15) = 0.90 ÷ 1.0925 = 0.824.

The plot runs to twice rated current. A starter usually holds the starting current to 125 to 200% of full load.

pages.name: Check
pages.task: A cumulative compound motor drives a shear. The coupling breaks and the load comes off. What does the speed do?
pages.answer: It rises to a definite no-load speed and holds there
pages.alt: The current falls, so the series part of the flux fades and the speed rises. The shunt part stays, so the flux holds up. The speed levels off at a definite no-load speed. On the picture at 15%, it rises from 1.00 to 1.224.
options: It runs away, like a series motor
It rises to a definite no-load speed and holds there
It hardly changes, like a shunt motor
pages.html: The current falls, so the series part of the flux fades and the speed rises. The shunt part stays, so the flux holds up. The speed levels off at a definite no-load speed. On the picture at 15%, it rises from 1.00 to 1.224.

pages.name: How it behaves
pages.text:
Starting torque: At the same current, higher than a shunt motor's and lower than a series motor's.

Running light: A definite no-load speed. Safe to run light while the shunt field is connected at full strength.

Speed regulation: Typically 15 to 25%. Some standard motors run about 30%. Better than a series motor's. It droops more than a shunt motor's.

Series share: More share, more starting torque and a higher no-load speed.

Reversing: Swap the armature leads, or both fields. Swap one field alone and it turns differential.

pages.name: Where it is used
pages.text:
Used for: Punch presses, shears, crushers and reciprocating compressors. Heavy loads that come and go.

Why: The series field takes the heavy stroke. The shunt field stops it racing when the load drops off.

Limits: Not for wide speed control by weakening the shunt field. The no-load speed can get very high. When it brakes by feeding power back, the armature current reverses through the series field. The fields then oppose, so such drives use a plain shunt motor. Brushes and commutator need regular care.

pages.name: Faults and tests
pages.text:
Safety first: Isolate, lock off and prove dead.

Series field reversed: It turns differential compound. The speed can rise with load and surge. A rebuild can reverse it.

Polarity: Check it against the maker's connection diagram. Never find it by running the motor light at full voltage.

Shunt field open: Only the series field is left. On a light load it can race like a series motor.

Sparking: Worn brushes, a rough commutator or an armature fault.

Tests: Megger the windings to frame. Measure the armature, series field and shunt field resistance.
pages.alt: isolator: open locked off and tagged megger windings frame ohmmeter series field brushes commutator

pages.name: Find the fault
pages.task: A compound motor is back from a rewind. Now its speed rises as the load goes on, and on a heavy load it surges. What is the most likely fault?
pages.answer: The series field is connected the wrong way round
pages.alt: A reversed series field subtracts from the shunt field. More load means less flux, so more speed. It has turned differential. Isolate and prove dead. Then check the series field connections against the maker's diagram. If they are right, check the brush position next.
options: The shunt field circuit is open
The series field is connected the wrong way round
pages.html: A reversed series field subtracts from the shunt field. More load means less flux, so more speed. It has turned differential. Isolate and prove dead. Then check the series field connections against the maker's diagram. If they are right, check the brush position next.
